title: Strategy is a boundary
body: A strategy is not a list of ambitions. It is a choice about where attention and resources will not go.
think_about: What are you keeping alive because you have not explicitly decided to stop it?

title: Activity is not the outcome
body: Busy teams can produce many visible outputs without changing the result that matters. Start with the change you hope to see, then choose the work.
think_about: Which recent task would look less important if you judged it by its outcome?

title: Requests are clues, not requirements
body: A requested feature often reveals a real frustration, but the requested solution may be only one guess at fixing it.
think_about: What problem is hidden beneath the last solution someone asked you for?

title: Feedback needs a loop
body: Collecting feedback is easy; closing the loop is useful. A system improves when observations change a next decision.
think_about: Where are you gathering information without deciding how it will alter your next move?

title: Simplicity preserves options
body: Every added rule, feature, or commitment creates future maintenance. Simplicity is often a way of keeping room to adapt.
think_about: What could you remove now that would make a later decision easier?

title: Incentives shape the system
body: People respond to what a system rewards, including the rewards nobody intended. Metrics can quietly become instructions.
think_about: What behaviour does one of your measures encourage as a side effect?

title: Second-order effects matter
body: A decision can solve the immediate problem while creating a slower, less visible one. Ask what happens after the first benefit arrives.
think_about: If your preferred option succeeds, what new constraint might it create?

title: Positioning is comparative
body: A useful description explains why someone should choose an option over the alternatives they actually have, including doing nothing.
think_about: What is the real alternative to the work you want someone to choose?

title: The printing press changed distribution
body: Movable-type printing lowered the cost of copying texts. Its power came not only from the machine, but from faster, wider circulation of ideas.
think_about: Which ideas change when copying and sharing become cheap?

title: Constantinople was a geographic advantage
body: The city sat beside the Bosporus, linking the Black Sea and Mediterranean. Geography made it a commercial and strategic hinge for centuries.
think_about: What location or connection gives an institution leverage beyond its size?

title: Containers made trade modular
body: Standard shipping containers reduced loading time, damage, and uncertainty. A humble standard reshaped ports, supply chains, and the geography of manufacturing.
think_about: Where would a shared standard remove costly hand-offs in your own work?
source_name: Smithsonian National Museum of American History

title: Institutions outlast personalities
body: The Roman Republic relied on offices, terms, and procedures rather than a single permanent ruler. Those arrangements were strengths, but also sites of conflict.
think_about: Which of your systems still works when its most capable person is absent?

title: Maps are arguments
body: Maps select, simplify, and emphasise. They can make borders, routes, resources, and distance appear more or less important than they are.
think_about: What does the map or dashboard you use make easy to notice—and easy to miss?

title: Public health is infrastructure
body: Nineteenth-century sanitation reforms showed that health outcomes can depend on water systems, streets, housing, and institutions—not only individual choices.
think_about: Which problem looks personal until you inspect the surrounding system?

title: Timekeeping coordinated industry
body: Railways helped make local solar time impractical for timetables. Standard time made coordination across distance more reliable.
think_about: What shared convention would reduce coordination friction for a group you know?
source_name: Smithsonian National Museum of American History

title: History includes path dependence
body: Early choices can become hard to reverse once tools, habits, and institutions grow around them. The best available option is not always the one that wins.
think_about: Which old decision still shapes your options mainly because changing it now feels expensive?

title: Confirmation bias narrows the search
body: People tend to seek and favour evidence that fits what they already believe. The bias is most useful to notice before a decision is final.
think_about: What evidence would genuinely make you change your mind?

title: Sunk costs are already spent
body: Past time or money can make an unpromising option feel harder to leave. The better question is what the next unit of effort is worth.
think_about: If you were starting today, would you choose this path again?

title: Availability is not frequency
body: Vivid or recent examples come to mind quickly, which can make them feel more common than they are.
think_about: What recent story is occupying more weight in your judgment than the wider evidence deserves?

title: Losses loom larger
body: The pain of losing something often weighs more heavily than an equivalent gain. This can make preserving the status quo feel safer than it is.
think_about: What potential loss are you protecting that may be distorting your choice?

title: Explain others carefully
body: We often explain another person’s behaviour through character while explaining our own through circumstance. Both views can miss useful context.
think_about: What situational constraint might you be overlooking in someone else’s behaviour?

title: Attention is a selection process
body: Attention does not merely illuminate what is there; it determines what receives further processing. What is outside the spotlight can still matter.
think_about: What important signal may be absent simply because your attention is allocated elsewhere?

title: Social proof is information
body: Other people’s choices can be useful evidence, especially under uncertainty. It becomes risky when popularity replaces independent judgment.
think_about: Where are you treating a crowd’s behaviour as proof rather than one input?

title: Habits use context
body: Repeated behaviour is often tied to a cue and environment, not just willpower. Changing the surrounding prompt can make a different action easier.
think_about: What cue reliably appears just before a habit you want to change?

title: Every choice has an opportunity cost
body: Choosing one use of time, money, or attention means giving up another. The cost is the value of the best forgone alternative.
think_about: What is the most valuable alternative you are declining with your current plan?

title: Incentives are not just money
body: Rules, status, convenience, and risk can all change behaviour. Good analysis asks what a person is rewarded or protected from doing.
think_about: What incentive is doing more work here than the stated rule?

title: Think at the margin
body: Many decisions are not all-or-nothing. The useful comparison is often the benefit and cost of one more unit, hour, or feature.
think_about: What changes if you ask whether the next increment is worth it rather than defending the whole project?

title: Prices carry scattered information
body: A price can reflect many local conditions that no single person sees completely. It is a signal, not a moral verdict.
think_about: What information might a rising or falling price be compressing?

title: Externalities leave someone else holding the cost
body: A decision can affect people who were not part of it. Pollution is the classic example, but time and attention can spill over too.
think_about: Who experiences a cost that your current decision does not record?

title: Comparative advantage is relative
body: Two people can both be good at a task, yet still gain by specialising according to what each gives up to do it.
think_about: What work are you competent at but not comparatively best placed to do?

title: Information can be asymmetric
body: One side of a transaction may know much more than the other. Trust, warranties, and reputation often exist to narrow that gap.
think_about: What does one party know here that the other cannot easily verify?

title: Networks can compound value
body: Some systems become more useful as more compatible participants join. The same dynamic can also make it costly to leave.
think_about: Which network effect helps you—and which one limits your options?

title: GPS needs relativity
body: Satellite clocks do not tick at exactly the same rate as clocks on Earth. Relativistic corrections are necessary for GPS to remain accurate.
think_about: What apparently abstract principle turns out to matter once a system becomes precise enough?

title: A semiconductor is a controlled switch
body: Transistors use materials whose electrical behaviour can be tuned. Billions of tiny switches arranged reliably make modern computing possible.
think_about: What complex system becomes clearer when you identify its simplest repeatable unit?

title: Vaccines train a response
body: Vaccination exposes the immune system to a safe representation of a threat, helping it recognise a later encounter more quickly.
think_about: Where could low-risk practice prepare you for a rarer high-stakes event?
source_name: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

title: Error correction makes systems practical
body: Communication and storage systems add structure so some errors can be detected or repaired. Reliability is often designed, not assumed.
think_about: Where would a small check catch an error before it becomes expensive?

title: Feedback can stabilise or amplify
body: Negative feedback counteracts change; positive feedback reinforces it. Engineers, ecosystems, and organisations all depend on knowing which loop is present.
think_about: Is the loop you are in correcting a deviation or making it larger?

title: Energy changes form
body: Energy is conserved, but useful energy can become more dispersed and harder to use. Efficiency is about directing some of that flow well.
think_about: Where is energy entering your system but leaving as avoidable waste?

title: A model is not the system
body: Scientific and engineering models deliberately omit detail to become useful. Their value depends on whether the omitted detail matters for the question.
think_about: What assumption in your current model would matter most if it were wrong?

title: Latency shapes behaviour
body: When a system responds slowly, people batch work, abandon attempts, or work around it. Performance changes the behaviour a design invites.
think_about: What workaround are people using that is really a signal about waiting time?

title: The metre is defined by light
body: The modern metre is defined by how far light travels in a vacuum during a specified fraction of a second, linking length to a physical constant.
think_about: What becomes easier to coordinate when a standard is tied to something reproducible?

title: Antarctica is a continent and a desert
body: Antarctica receives very little precipitation in its interior. Cold does not prevent a place from meeting the definition of a desert.
think_about: Which category do you picture too narrowly because one typical example dominates it?

title: Octopuses have distributed control
body: Much of an octopus’s nervous system is in its arms, allowing local sensing and movement without every detail being directed centrally.
think_about: What work could be handled closer to where the information first appears?

title: Time zones are coordination tools
body: They are social agreements layered on top of Earth’s rotation. Political borders and practical ties help explain their irregular shapes.
think_about: Which convention in your life exists mainly because coordination matters more than perfect representation?

title: Honey can last remarkably well
body: Low water content and acidity make honey difficult for many microbes to grow in. Storage conditions still matter, but the chemistry is unusually protective.
think_about: What property of a system makes it resilient without constant intervention?

title: The Moon is slowly receding
body: Tidal interactions transfer energy and cause the Moon’s average distance from Earth to increase by a small amount over time.
think_about: What slow process would look important if you viewed it over decades instead of days?

title: Maps can put any direction at the top
body: North-up maps are a convention, not a physical requirement. Orientation changes what feels central, peripheral, or intuitive.
think_about: What changes when you rotate the frame through which you view a problem?

title: A day is not always exactly 24 hours
body: Earth’s rotation varies slightly, while civil time is kept uniform enough for modern coordination. Timekeeping is both astronomical and engineered.
think_about: Where do you rely on a tidy approximation that conceals small real variation?

title: Control and response
body: Stoic philosophy distinguishes between what is up to us and what is not. The point is not passivity; it is directing effort toward judgments and actions you can shape.
think_about: What part of this situation is genuinely within your next action?

title: The examined life
body: Socratic inquiry treats confidence as an invitation to test reasons. A good question can reveal where a belief rests on habit rather than understanding.
think_about: Which belief of yours would benefit from one more honest question?

title: Know thyself
body: The Delphic maxim is less a demand for a fixed identity than a prompt to notice limits, motives, and assumptions.
think_about: What do you reliably do well—and what condition makes you less reliable?

title: Uncertainty is not ignorance
body: Good judgment can recognise degrees of confidence. Being able to say “I do not know yet” can be more useful than a premature certainty.
think_about: Where could you replace a forced yes-or-no answer with a clearer level of confidence?

title: Means and ends
body: A worthwhile outcome does not automatically justify every route toward it. Ethics asks us to examine methods as well as goals.
think_about: Would you still endorse this approach if everyone used it in similar circumstances?

title: Attention is a value judgment
body: What you repeatedly attend to becomes part of the shape of your life. Attention is limited, so allocation is never entirely neutral.
think_about: What receives your best attention by default, and is that a choice you endorse?

title: A life can contain competing goods
body: Many difficult choices are not between good and bad, but between values that cannot all be maximised at once.
think_about: Which two good things are you treating as though they could be fully reconciled without a trade-off?

title: Revision is intellectual strength
body: Changing a view after better evidence is not inconsistency. It is the ordinary cost of taking truth more seriously than pride.
think_about: What opinion would be easier to revise if nobody were keeping score?

body: Reversible decisions is useful because it changes how an organisation allocates limited attention. It reveals a trade-off that can stay hidden when work is judged only by activity.
